Explore psychology

The map of psychology

Areas of knowledge, applied branches, schools and key figures. A wide catalogue with simple navigation.

16 areas

Areas of knowledge

Each area has three reading levels: a short introduction, a fuller explanation and an extension with references.

Core processes

Perception

How the senses and the brain turn stimuli into a world of objects, distances and meaning. Includes illusions, face recognition and perceptual experience.

Three reading levels →Core processes

Attention

Why we cannot process everything at once: selection, distraction, sustained concentration and what happens when we do two things at once.

Three reading levels →Core processes

Learning

How behaviour changes with experience: conditioning, observational learning, deliberate practice and skill acquisition.

Three reading levels →Core processes

Memory

How we store, keep and retrieve information, why we forget and why we sometimes remember things that did not happen that way.

Three reading levels →Core processes

Thinking

Reasoning, problem solving, decision-making, beliefs and the mental shortcuts that sometimes lead us astray.

Three reading levels →Core processes

Language

How we learn to speak, how we understand and produce sentences, non-verbal communication and bilingualism.

Three reading levels →Core processes

Motivation

What moves us to act: goals, incentives, persistence, habits and self-regulation.

Three reading levels →Core processes

Emotion

What emotions are, how they are expressed, what role context plays and how we regulate them.

Three reading levels →Person and development

Personality

Traits, temperament, identity and self-concept: what is relatively stable in each person and what changes.

Three reading levels →Person and development

Intelligence and creativity

Models of intelligence, how it is assessed, what creativity is and why these topics still spark debate.

Three reading levels →Core processes

Biological psychology

Biological bases of behaviour: nervous system, hormones, genes and environment, evolution.

Three reading levels →Core processes

Neuropsychology

What brain injury and brain function teach us about memory, language, attention and behaviour.

Three reading levels →Person and development

Development

Changes and continuities across the whole lifespan, from birth to old age.

Three reading levels →Relationships

Social psychology

How others influence us: identity, attitudes, prejudice, cooperation, conformity and groups.

Three reading levels →Methods

Methods and statistics

How psychology is researched: designs, samples, uncertainty, correlation and causation, replication.

Three reading levels →Methods

Psychometrics and assessment

How psychology measures: reliability, validity, norms, interviews and responsible interpretation of results.

Three reading levels →

Key figures

Biographies

1832–1920

Wilhelm Wundt

German physician and philosopher. He organised one of the first psychology laboratories in Leipzig and trained a generation of researchers from around the world.

1842–1910

William James

American physician, psychologist and philosopher. His Principles of Psychology (1890) described consciousness as a stream and shaped generations of readers.

1863–1930

Mary Whiton Calkins

American psychologist and philosopher. She completed every requirement for a Harvard doctorate, which was refused because she was a woman, and was the first woman to preside over the American Psychological Association.

1871–1939

Margaret Floy Washburn

American psychologist, the first woman to earn a doctorate in psychology (Cornell, 1894). Her book The Animal Mind was a standard text in comparative psychology.

1849–1936

Iván Pávlov

Russian physiologist, winner of the 1904 Nobel Prize in Medicine for his work on digestion. While studying salivation in dogs he described the conditioned reflex, the basis of classical conditioning.

1896–1980

Jean Piaget

Swiss biologist and epistemologist. He studied how children construct knowledge and proposed one of the most influential theories of development of the twentieth century.

1913–1999

Mary Ainsworth

American-Canadian developmental psychologist. She observed families in Uganda and Baltimore, created the Strange Situation and described children's attachment styles.

1902–1977

Alexander Luria

Soviet neuropsychologist. A colleague of Vygotsky, he studied how culture shapes thinking and founded modern neuropsychology through his work with soldiers wounded in the Second World War.

n. 1944

Elizabeth Loftus

American psychologist. Her experiments showed that memories can be altered by later information, with direct consequences for trials and eyewitness testimony.

1928–2012

Ulric Neisser

German-born American psychologist. His book Cognitive Psychology (1967) gave the field its name, and he later argued for studying memory and perception in real life.

1937–1996

Amos Tversky

Israeli cognitive psychologist. With Daniel Kahneman he showed that people judge and decide using mental shortcuts that produce systematic biases, and together they formulated prospect theory.
